power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Selecting an appropriate questionnaire to measure autistic traits in children for research or clinical practice requires considering several factors.

These include the validity of the questionnaire's structure, the questionnaire's sensitivity and specificity, the extent to which autistic traits are represented (e.g., whether all diagnostic sub-criteria are adequately represented), the clarity and respectfulness of item wording, and inclusive research practices used during questionnaire development.

To provide clinicians and researchers information on the most sensitive, specific, and contemporary measures for identifying and assessing autistic traits, we conducted a review of existing caregiver-report questionnaires for measuring autistic traits in children aged 4-12 years.
Method: Ten questionnaires were identified for inclusion.

For each included questionnaire, targeted searches were conducted in the form of forward citation searches to identify peer-reviewed studies reporting on the instrument's development or subsequent psychometric evaluation (factor or component analysis, sensitivity, specificity).

Results: Overall, there was marked variability in the extent to which questionnaires assess autistic traits across diagnostic sub-criteria, as well as in their sensitivity and specificity for differentiating autism from various other groups.
Several questionnaires lacked psychometric support for their proposed structure.
Respectfulness and clarity of item wording could be improved in most questionnaires.
Autism community input during questionnaire development was typically limited or absent.
Of note, the recently developed Autism Symptom Dimensions Questionnaire stood out as a promising freely available measure.

Discussion: Developers of new questionnaires should use inclusive research practices, write items using clear and respectful language, ensure adequate psychometric properties, and aim to include items from all diagnostic sub-criteria.
The efficiency and accessibility of questionnaires makes them a valuable tool in timeand resource-limited environments (Trevethan, 2017).

text.text: However, the implications of questionnaire selection, whether it be for either of these purposes, should not be understated.

In research contexts, these tools are commonly used to operationalise and quantify autistic traits, supporting investigations into the distribution of autistic traits across the general population and exploration of how certain behaviours change across development (e.g., Pender et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In research contexts, these tools are commonly used to operationalise and quantify autistic traits, supporting investigations into the distribution of autistic traits across the general population and exploration of how certain behaviours change across development (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Pender et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such studies have played a pivotal role in shaping our current understanding of autism.

Notably, studies examining the relationships between autistic traits (e.g., Huerta et al., 2012) contributed to the development of the current diagnostic criteria for autism outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR; American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
text.formatted: Notably, studies examining the relationships between autistic traits (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Huerta et al., 2012)</ref> contributed to the development of the current diagnostic criteria for autism outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR; American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

text.text: However, rigorous, high-quality research depends on the validity and appropriateness of the measures used, thus the selection of psychometrically sound questionnaires grounded in current theoretical frameworks is essential in continuing to advance our understanding of autism.
Concurrently, autism questionnaires are widely used in clinical practice as screening tools to indicate whether a formal diagnostic assessment may be warranted (Thabtah & Peebles, 2019).
text.formatted: Concurrently, autism questionnaires are widely used in clinical practice as screening tools to indicate whether a formal diagnostic assessment may be warranted <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Thabtah & Peebles, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Because autism can be diagnosed through a variety of trait combinations, a questionnaire used for screening which focuses on only a subset of diagnostic sub-criteria may fail to identify individuals who present differently.

Put differently, if certain sub-criteria are not represented in the items of a questionnaire, some individuals showing traits or behaviour consistent with those sub-criteria may not obtain a score considered high enough to prompt referral for a full diagnostic evaluation.

Therefore, improper selection of a questionnaire could be a contributing factor in the high estimates of missed autism diagnoses reported in the literature (e.g., Cooper et al., 2017; Wiggins et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Therefore, improper selection of a questionnaire could be a contributing factor in the high estimates of missed autism diagnoses reported in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cooper et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Wiggins et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These considerations are particularly relevant during the primary school years (approximately ages 4 to 12), which is an especially important period for identifying and measuring autistic traits.
Autism research is most frequently conducted on child populations (Mason et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Autism research is most frequently conducted on child populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Mason et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This developmental stage also aligns with the most common age of autism diagnosis identified in a recent meta-analysis of international data (Van 'T Hof et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This developmental stage also aligns with the most common age of autism diagnosis identified in a recent meta-analysis of international data (Van 'T <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Hof et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the prevalence of autism is highest among Australian children aged 5 to 12 years (Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2024), while a large-scale cross-sectional study in the United Stated reported the highest rate of autism diagnoses among 5-to 8-year-olds (Grosvenor et al., 2024).

text.text: Similarly, Scottish census data indicate the prevalence of autism increases with age until around 10-11 years, reflecting the typical timing of diagnosis (Rydzewska et al., 2019).

text.text: During this developmental period, children often lack the abilities required to reliably report on their own experiences.
As a result, caregivers are typically the primary informants in both clinical and research settings.
Caregiver-report questionnaires therefore represent a particularly appropriate and commonly used method for measuring autistic traits in this age group.

We suggest that researchers or clinicians selecting a caregiver-report questionnaire for identifying and measuring autistic traits in primary school aged children should consider the five characteristics summarised below, weighing these in accordance with the aims of the questionnaire's use.
When selecting a questionnaire, its psychometric adequacy must be considered.
Psychometric adequacy refers to statistical properties which determine if a questionnaire fits its intended purpose, be it for research or clinical use.

Two such properties are (a) psychometric support for scale structure and (b) the sensitivity and specificity of the questionnaire (i.e., the capacity to correctly identify who is autistic and who is non-autistic, respectively).

Questionnaires that demonstrate sound scale structure have typically been subjected to factor analysis to determine the number and nature of dimensions (factors) within the construct being measured (Boateng et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Questionnaires that demonstrate sound scale structure have typically been subjected to factor analysis to determine the number and nature of dimensions (factors) within the construct being measured <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Boateng et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Factor analysis refers primarily to Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA; Yong & Pearce, 2013).
text.formatted: Factor analysis refers primarily to Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Yong & Pearce, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Sometimes Exploratory Structural Equation Modelling (ESEM; Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009) is used instead of either EFA or CFA.
text.formatted: Sometimes Exploratory Structural Equation Modelling (ESEM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Asparouhov & Muthén, 2009)</ref> is used instead of either EFA or CFA.

text.text: ESEM freely estimates cross-loadings, as with EFA, but can evaluate model fit, as with CFA.
Alternatively, Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is sometimes used instead of EFA.
PCA functions differently in that it does not separate specific variance and error variance, instead seeking to explain total variance.
This can limit the generalisability of the derived component structure (Tavakol & Wetzel, 2020).
text.formatted: This can limit the generalisability of the derived component structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Tavakol & Wetzel, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Given this, the use of PCA instead of EFA is controversial (Loewen & Gonulal, 2015).
text.formatted: Given this, the use of PCA instead of EFA is controversial <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Loewen & Gonulal, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, this review will include PCA where it has been used in the analysis of scale structure.

Regardless of the statistical approach applied, typically, an exploratory technique should initially be used to derive a factor structure, which then forms the a priori model for further evaluation through a confirmatory technique (Morgado et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Regardless of the statistical approach applied, typically, an exploratory technique should initially be used to derive a factor structure, which then forms the a priori model for further evaluation through a confirmatory technique <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Morgado et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: If a wellestablished model already exists, using a confirmatory technique directly is appropriate.

The absence of psychometric support for scale structure calls into question the validity with which one can infer that the observed scores reflect the theoretical constructs they are supposedly measuring.
Therefore, it is good practice to use the derived factor structure to inform the formation of questionnaire subscales and where this is not the case, clear justification should be provided.

In addition to ensuring psychometric support for scale structure, good to excellent sensitivity and specificity must be established if the questionnaire is to be used for screening purposes (Swift et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In addition to ensuring psychometric support for scale structure, good to excellent sensitivity and specificity must be established if the questionnaire is to be used for screening purposes <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Swift et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of autism screeners, sensitivity is the likelihood of correctly identifying autistic people, whereas specificity is the likelihood of correctly identifying non-autistic people.
Sensitivity and specificity trade off against each other (e.g. a low cutoff score would favour sensitivity at the expense of specificity, and vice-versa for a high cutoff score).
It is important to understand which autistic traits a questionnaire is measuring when deciding whether to use it.

Based on the DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), the core diagnostic criteria of autism are persistent differences and difficulties in social interaction and communication (Criterion A), and patterns of highly focused or repetitive behaviours, speech, or interests, or sensory processing differences (Criterion B).

As shown in Table 1, there are three sub-criteria for Criterion A and four sub-criteria for Criterion B. An autism diagnosis requires that all three of the Criterion A sub-criteria and at least two of the four Criterion B sub-criteria are met.

An autism diagnosis requires that all three of the Criterion A sub-criteria and at least two of the four Criterion B sub-criteria are met.

text.text: While we acknowledge some associated autistic features may fall outside the formal diagnostic criteria, the present review aims to evaluate questionnaires within the context of current diagnostic practices.

For this reason, we focus on the DSM-5-TR, though we consider our assessment of autistic trait coverage similarly applicable to the International Classification of Diseases, eleventh edition, criteria (World Health Organization, 2022), given the concordance between the two diagnostic systems.
text.formatted: For this reason, we focus on the DSM-5-TR, though we consider our assessment of autistic trait coverage similarly applicable to the International Classification of Diseases, eleventh edition, criteria <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2022)</ref>, given the concordance between the two diagnostic systems.

text.text: The wording of questionnaire items is critical for ensuring their usefulness, reliability, and validity.
Ambiguous or complex items may lead to inaccurate responses, skipped questions, or respondents abandoning the questionnaire entirely (Nicolaidis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Ambiguous or complex items may lead to inaccurate responses, skipped questions, or respondents abandoning the questionnaire entirely <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Nicolaidis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Further, ambiguous items can worsen the psychometric properties of the questionnaire due to respondents interpreting the items' meanings differently than intended, while technical and jargon-heavy language limits the accessibility of questionnaires (Clark & Watson, 2016).
text.formatted: Further, ambiguous items can worsen the psychometric properties of the questionnaire due to respondents interpreting the items' meanings differently than intended, while technical and jargon-heavy language limits the accessibility of questionnaires <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark & Watson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, in autistic trait questionnaires, it is important to avoid non-literal language (e.g., metaphors, turns of phrase), which autistic people often find challenging to interpret (Nicolaidis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Additionally, in autistic trait questionnaires, it is important to avoid non-literal language (e.g., metaphors, turns of phrase), which autistic people often find challenging to interpret <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Nicolaidis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This point remains pertinent in caregiver-report questionnaires, given respondents may be autistic or have autistic traits themselves, due to the high heritability of autism (Sandin et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This point remains pertinent in caregiver-report questionnaires, given respondents may be autistic or have autistic traits themselves, due to the high heritability of autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Sandin et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Using respectful neurodiversity-affirmative language in the wording of items is also important due to potential implications for response accuracy, as well as wider societal consequences.

Language referring exclusively to impairments and difficulties can reduce the accuracy of responses due to social desirability bias (Tourangeau, 2018) and risks offering a prejudiced understanding of what "autistic traits" encompass (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Language referring exclusively to impairments and difficulties can reduce the accuracy of responses due to social desirability bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Tourangeau, 2018)</ref> and risks offering a prejudiced understanding of what "autistic traits" encompass <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: At the societal level, the use of deficit-based language in both research and clinical practice, rooted in a medical model of autism, gave rise to the earlier public view of autism as a disease (Kapp et al., 2013).
text.formatted: At the societal level, the use of deficit-based language in both research and clinical practice, rooted in a medical model of autism, gave rise to the earlier public view of autism as a disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Kapp et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Concurrently, this public view of autism, legitimised by the deficit-based language used by researchers and clinicians, contributed to the marginalisation and discrimination against autistic people (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Concurrently, this public view of autism, legitimised by the deficit-based language used by researchers and clinicians, contributed to the marginalisation and discrimination against autistic people <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, as the use of language within research and clinical practice has clear societal consequences, there is an ethical obligation to employ respectful language throughout.
This includes the wording of autistic trait questionnaires.

Referred to as a "hallmark of excellence in research" in a recent editorial (pg. 1501 , Fletcher-Watson, Bölte, et al., 2021), inclusive research practices (also termed "participatory research") refer to research which is done with autistic people, rather than done on them (Israel et al., 2005).

text.text: There are different levels of inclusive engagement of autistic people in research, such as partnership/co-production or consultation (Arnstein, 1969; den Houting et al., 2021).
text.formatted: There are different levels of inclusive engagement of autistic people in research, such as partnership/co-production or consultation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Arnstein, 1969;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">den Houting et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to being morally and ethically right (Fletcher-Watson, Brook, et al., 2021; Wright et al., 2014), including autistic people in research decisions, methodology design, and the interpretation of findings benefits research in many ways (Keating, 2021).
text.formatted: In addition to being morally and ethically right <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fletcher-Watson, Brook, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Wright et al., 2014)</ref>, including autistic people in research decisions, methodology design, and the interpretation of findings benefits research in many ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Keating, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For example, inclusive practices in questionnaire development can help ensure the items reflect the actual experiences of autistic people (Nicolaidis et al., 2019 (Nicolaidis et al., , 2020) ) as well as offer insight into the respectfulness and clarity of items.
text.formatted: For example, inclusive practices in questionnaire development can help ensure the items reflect the actual experiences of autistic people <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Nicolaidis et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Nicolaidis et al., , 2020) )</ref> as well as offer insight into the respectfulness and clarity of items.

text.text: Further, while inclusive research practices are not in themselves a statistical method, they do have direct and important implications for the psychometrics of the questionnaire as they are key in ensuring content validity; that is, the extent to which items measure the construct they are meant to.

Research synthesising and critically appraising existing questionnaires against the above characteristics is necessary to provide clinicians and researchers with information on the most sensitive, specific, and contemporary measures for identifying and assessing autistic traits.
While several reviews of autistic trait questionnaires exist, these have generally addressed narrower or different questions from those considered in the present review.

For example, Norris and Lecavalier (2010) reviewed the diagnostic accuracy of five caregiver completed Level 2 screening measures, while Chesnut and colleagues (2017) focused specifically on the screening accuracy of the Social Communication Questionnaire.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Norris and Lecavalier (2010)</ref> reviewed the diagnostic accuracy of five caregiver completed Level 2 screening measures, while <ref type="bibr">Chesnut and colleagues (2017)</ref> focused specifically on the screening accuracy of the Social Communication Questionnaire.

text.text: Hirota and colleagues (2018) examined the validity of screening tools for children and adults, and Fekar Gharamaleki and colleagues (2021) provided a broader descriptive review of autism screening tests, including their administration, scoring, and reported psychometric properties.

Therefore, although previous reviews provide valuable information regarding the availability and diagnostic performance of autism questionnaires, they do not comprehensively evaluate how contemporary caregiver-report questionnaires for children were developed, how well questionnaire content represents the current diagnostic construct of autism, or the adequacy of their underlying measurement structure.
Furthermore, while DSM criterion coverage has received some attention in previous literature, it has not been systematically evaluated across caregiver-report autistic trait questionnaires.

For example, Thabtah and Peebles (2019) identified DSM-5 fulfilment as one of the characteristics considered in their review and concluded that many existing screening measures did not fully represent DSM-5 criteria.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Thabtah and Peebles (2019)</ref> identified DSM-5 fulfilment as one of the characteristics considered in their review and concluded that many existing screening measures did not fully represent DSM-5 criteria.

text.text: However, they did not report a systematic procedure for evaluating criterion coverage, such as mapping questionnaire items to individual DSM-5 criteria, and they did not provide questionnaire-level results demonstrating the extent of coverage.
Indeed, they subsequently identified such item-to-criterion mapping as an important area for future work.

Criterion-level analysis has been undertaken for some standardised diagnostic instruments: for example, Evers and colleagues (2021) mapped items from three standardised diagnostic instruments onto DSM-5 sub-criteria, identifying substantial variation in how these diagnostic instruments represented the criteria.
However, their analysis did not extend to caregiver-report questionnaires.

Consequently, to the best of our knowledge, there is no existing review that has systematically evaluated criterion-level DSM-5-TR coverage across caregiver-report questionnaires for autistic traits in children.

Similarly, existing reviews do not offer substantive insight into the adequacy of the analysis of scale structure of the questionnaires or the use of inclusive research practices in questionnaire development.
Further, there is no existing review which assesses the clarity and respectfulness of item wording in existing questionnaires.

Therefore, the present review critically analyses and synthesises research on the development and subsequent psychometric evaluation of existing caregiver-report questionnaires for measuring autistic traits in children (aged 4 to 12 years) against these characteristics.
The literature search was conducted in two phases: (1) search for relevant autism questionnaires; and (2) search for studies reporting the development or evaluation of those measures.
Both of the search phases were conducted by author GH.
A conventional PRISMA search strategy was considered.
However, due to wide variability in potential terminology (e.g., "Autis*", "Asperger*", "PDD-NOS", combined with "tool", "scale", "inventory", etc.
), trial systematic searches returned thousands of irrelevant hits.
For example, a single Web of Science search string produced over 14,000 records.

Following librarian consultation, and drawing on methods used in a prior review (Hayden-Evans et al., 2022), we instead identified relevant caregiver questionnaires via multiple sources: Relevant caregiver questionnaires were initially identified via internet searches, websites of major publishers (Pearson, WPS), existing reviews (e.g., Fekar Gharamaleki et al., 2021; Thabtah & Peebles, 2019), the test libraries of a local children's institute and a university clinic for training clinical psychologists and neuropsychologists, and measures known to the authors (researchers and clinicians working in the field of autism).

text.text: Questionnaires were included in the review if they were: (1) available and designed for use in English; (2) autism focused (e.g., rather than an autism subscale of a larger questionnaire); (3) caregiver report; (4) developed for use with school age children (4-to 12years-old); (5) developed after the release of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV; American Psychiatric Association, 1994); (6) accessible to the research team (where a measure was not freely available and not available within either of the local test libraries, the authors and publishers were contacted for access); and (7) not an older version of an otherwise included questionnaire.
It is important to note that questionnaires did not need to be developed as screeners to be included in the review.
This was to ensure the inclusion of common questionnaires used in autism research.

The decision to include questionnaires developed after the release of the previous diagnostic framework (i.e., the DSM-IV) rather than the introduction of the current diagnostic framework (i.e., the DSM-5) was to ensure the inclusion of the most commonly used measures to date.

Measures were not included if they were: (1) reported only in grey literature; (2) a version of an original English questionnaire adapted for use in a different language; or (3) an adapted version of an existing questionnaire otherwise eligible for inclusion (e.g., a shortened version).

Targeted searches were conducted to identify peer-reviewed studies reporting on the development or subsequent psychometric evaluation (factor or component analysis, sensitivity, specificity) of the included questionnaires.
Again, a conventional search strategy was initially considered.
We trialled targeted systematic searches for each questionnaire (using full titles and acronyms, combined with psychometric terms such as "factor analysis").
However, this approach was inconsistent in performance.
For some measures, acronyms are common words (e.g., "AIM" for the Autism Impact Measure), yielding over a million irrelevant hits within a single database.
For others, using only the full title missed key papers that referred to the questionnaire solely by acronym.
Running multiple such searches across databases resulted in impractically large numbers of records (in the thousands per measure).
Therefore, a less conventional, though still systematic and rigorous, approach was conducted.
This involved forward citation searches for each questionnaire using Google Scholar.
All searches were conducted on December 29 th , 2025.
For studies reporting on factor or component analysis, data were extracted on sample size, age range, gender, ethnicity, IQ, and diagnostic status of participants.
For studies evaluating sensitivity and specificity, information on age range, comparison group type, and sample size was extracted.
All studies describing the development of the questionnaires were inspected for explicit mention of inclusive research practices.

The items of each questionnaire included in the review were independently inspected and sorted into the seven diagnostic sub-criteria of the DSM-5-TR by the first and fifth authors, a clinical psychologist registrar and a clinical neuropsychologist.

Items were either (1) allocated to a single sub-criterion, (2) assessed as tapping more than one diagnostic subcriterion and so marked as "More than one", or (3) could not be categorised under a single sub-criterion or "More than one" and so were marked as "Unclear/None".

This last category occasionally included items which were assessing behaviours or traits associated with autism but not part of the diagnostic criteria (e.g., an item asking whether the child tends to focus on details).
Inter-rater reliability was calculated as percentage agreement.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion.
Items were first independently reviewed for wording clarity by two non-autistic authors.
Inter-rater reliability was calculated as percentage agreement.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion and when necessary, brought to two additional non-autistic authors.
Items were then independently reviewed for wording clarity by an autistic author.
This review was compared against the consensus decision reached by the two non-autistic authors.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion.

Clarity of wording was coded as "Acceptable" (i.e., no issues with clarity), "Unclear Wording/Meaning" (i.e., contained technical jargon, such as "idiosyncratic", and/or could reasonably be interpreted in several different ways, such as "becomes upset in a situation with lots of things going on"), "Double-Barrelled" (i.e., a single item enquiring about more than one behaviour, such as "does s/he prefer imaginative activities such as play-acting or storytelling, rather than numbers or lists of facts"), "Internal Experience" (i.e., an item which is asking about a child's internal experience and therefore not observable by an informant, such as "if s/he tries to imagine something, s/he finds it very easy to create a picture in her/his mind") or "Other" (i.e., issue with clarity not otherwise captured, such as referring to the dated social game The Mulberry Bush).
We considered questionnaires with at least 90% of items coded as "Acceptable" as having satisfactory clarity.
Flesch Reading Ease (FRE; Flesch, 1979) was also calculated using Microsoft Word (Microsoft Corporation, 2024) to offer a standardized rating of readability.
text.formatted: Flesch Reading Ease (FRE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Flesch, 1979)</ref> was also calculated using Microsoft Word <ref type="bibr">(Microsoft Corporation, 2024)</ref> to offer a standardized rating of readability.

text.text: FRE is based on the average number of words and syllables per sentence in a given passage, with fewer words per sentence and fewer syllables per word resulting in a higher FRE rating.
A FRE rating of 60 indicates a 'standard' reading level, equivalent to an 8 th or 9 th grade reading level (Flesch, 1979).
text.formatted: A FRE rating of 60 indicates a 'standard' reading level, equivalent to an 8 th or 9 th grade reading level <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Flesch, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, scores of 60 or above were considered acceptable, with a higher score indicating the questionnaire is easier to read.
However, while FRE can provide a general idea of reading difficulty, it should not be confused with understandability.
A short sentence containing only one syllable words may still be nonsensical, irrespective of a high FRE.
Therefore, it is beneficial to consider the FRE in combination with our assessment of clarity.
To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing standardised methodology for assessing the use of respectful and neurodiversity-affirming language in item wording.
Therefore, we drew from available guidance on respectful and neurodiversity-affirming language use (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021; Dwyer et al., 2022; Monk, 2022).
text.formatted: Therefore, we drew from available guidance on respectful and neurodiversity-affirming language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Dwyer et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Monk, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Items were coded as "Appropriate" (i.e., no issues with respectfulness), "Could be Improved" (i.e., used potentially insensitive wording for which there are respectful alternatives, such as "rigid" or "inflexible"), or "Problematic" (i.e., used clearly insensitive language, and/or upheld harmful and inaccurate stereotypes about autistic people, such as lacking empathy).
As with item clarity, items were first independently reviewed by two non-autistic authors.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion and when necessary, brought to two additional non-autistic authors.
Items were then independently reviewed by an autistic author.
This review was compared against the consensus decision reached by the two non-autistic authors.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion.
Inter-rater reliability was calculated as percentage agreement.
We considered questionnaires with at least 90% of items coded as "Appropriate" as adequately respectful.

text.text: Unlike the other questionnaires, the AIM's intended purpose is to detect small short-term behavioural changes.

As such, each item is rated on two 5-point Likert scales (Frequency: how often the behaviour occurred within the past two weeks; and Impact: how much the behaviour interfered with the child's everyday functioning over the past two weeks).
Only a total score (i.e., summed frequency and impact scores) is calculated, and the authors did not propose subscales.

text.text: The CAST (Scott et al., 2002) is a 37-item caregiver-report questionnaire for screening autistic traits in 4-to 11-year-old children.
text.formatted: The CAST <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Scott et al., 2002)</ref> is a 37-item caregiver-report questionnaire for screening autistic traits in 4-to 11-year-old children.

text.text: However, six items are control questions on general development with the 31 remaining items used in the total score calculation.
Respondents indicate the presence or absence (yes or no) of behaviours in the context of the child's developmental history.
There are no proposed subscales.

text.text: The SCDC (Skuse et al., 1997) is a 12-item caregiver-report questionnaire for measuring autistic traits in 5-to 17-year-old children.
text.formatted: The SCDC <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Skuse et al., 1997)</ref> is a 12-item caregiver-report questionnaire for measuring autistic traits in 5-to 17-year-old children.

text.text: Respondents rate the accuracy of each item in describing the child's behaviour over the past six months, using a 3-point Likert scale (from0 = Not true to2 = Very or often true).

Although there are no proposed subscales, nine of the items are purported to measure reciprocal social interaction and communication skills, with the remaining three measuring behavioural difficulties more generally.

Originally developed as the Autism Screening Questionnaire (Berument et al., 1999), the SCQ (Rutter et al., 2003) is a 40-item caregiver-report questionnaire for screening autistic traits in individuals aged 4+ years.
text.formatted: Originally developed as the Autism Screening Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Berument et al., 1999)</ref>, the SCQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Rutter et al., 2003)</ref> is a 40-item caregiver-report questionnaire for screening autistic traits in individuals aged 4+ years.

text.text: However, as the first item simply documents whether the individual can speak in short phases or sentences, only 39 items contribute to scoring.
Respondents indicate the presence or absence of behaviours using a yes/no response format.

When the Autism Screening Questionnaire was published as the SCQ, two versions were made available: the Current form, which asks about behaviours within the past three months, and the Lifetime form, which asks about behaviours throughout the individual's developmental history.

text.text: Though the website indicates the additional 13items are language-based items suitable for verbal children, there is no information provided on how these additional items were created or whether they have been psychometrically validated.
Regardless, research utilising the SSDS has alternately used either the 58-item or 71-item version (e.g., Frazier, Khaliq, et al., 2023; Frazier, Whitehouse, et al., 2023).

text.text: Consequently, we present information on both versions.

The SSDS contains five subscales using 40 of the 58-items: Social Motivation (14 items), Social Affiliation (8 items), Expressive Social Communication (7 items), Social Recognition (7 items), and Unusual Approach (4 items).

Forward citation searches using Google Scholar for each included questionnaire yielded a total of 11,716 results: ABII-PQ (n = 17), AIM (n = 139), AQ-Child (n = 820), ASDQ (n = 16), CAST (n = 612), GARS-3 (n = 810), SCDC (n = 989), SCQ (n = 1,932), SRS-2 (n = 6,333), SSDS (n = 48).

Screening of these citations identified 51 peer-reviewed studies reporting on the development or subsequent psychometric evaluation (factor or component analysis, sensitivity, specificity) of the included questionnaires.
We narratively summarise analytic work on the scale structure for each questionnaire (e.g., EFA, PCA, ESEM) and note whether the analysis supports the proposed structure of the given questionnaire.

text.text: No scale structure analytic work could be located for the ABII-PQ.
Five studies reported factor analysis on the AIM for autistic samples.
The original AIM development study favoured an EFA-derived four-factor model that included 25 of the 41 items (Kanne et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The original AIM development study favoured an EFA-derived four-factor model that included 25 of the 41 items <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Kanne et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, four subsequent studies have demonstrated consistent support through EFAs and CFAs for a five-factor model using 29 of the 41 items (Grimm et al., 2023; Houghton et al., 2019; Mazurek et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, four subsequent studies have demonstrated consistent support through EFAs and CFAs for a five-factor model using 29 of the 41 items <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Grimm et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Houghton et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Mazurek et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Zhong et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, this 29-item five-factor model demonstrated measurement invariance across sex (Zhong et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Furthermore, this 29-item five-factor model demonstrated measurement invariance across sex <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Zhong et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the research on the AIM to date suggests a 29-item version of the questionnaire with five subscales (Repetitive Behaviour, Communication, Atypical Behaviour, Social Reciprocity, and Peer Interaction) would have stronger construct validity than the existing 41-item version.

In the initial development of the AQ-Child (Auyeung et al., 2008) with autistic and non-autistic children, three items were deemed difficult to assess in young children and were eliminated from subsequent analysis.
text.formatted: In the initial development of the AQ-Child <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Auyeung et al., 2008)</ref> with autistic and non-autistic children, three items were deemed difficult to assess in young children and were eliminated from subsequent analysis.

text.text: The 47 remaining items were submitted to PCA.

A four-component solution ─ Mind-Reading (16 items), Attention to Detail (9 items), Social Skills (15 items), and Imagination (7 items) ─ was identified as optimal. Auyeung and colleagues (2008) reported that these components were highly correlated with four of their five original, theoretically derived subscales (Communication, Attention to Detail, Social Skills, and Imagination).

text.text: Although three of the component names are identical to three of the subscale names, it is important to note the items that mapped onto these components do not align with the subscales.

A subsequent study by Gomez and colleagues (2019) used CFA in an ADHD child sample to test Auyeung and colleagues' (2008) 47-item four-factor model as well as the fivefactor model (with all 50 items) corresponding to the theoretically proposed subscales.

text.text: Results indicated poor fit for either model.
Subsequently, Gomez and colleagues conducted EFA for one to five-factor models (using 47 items) and found support for a four-factor model using 32 items.

While there is a lack of consistency between the results of the two scale-structure analytic studies conducted on the AQ-Child, neither provides support for the purported five subscale (with 10 items per subscale) structure of the questionnaire.

The development of the ASDQ included exploratory and confirmatory ESEMs, and CFA, to investigate its psychometric structure, with support reported for a nine-factor model with an additional general factor (i.e., bifactor; Frazier et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The development of the ASDQ included exploratory and confirmatory ESEMs, and CFA, to investigate its psychometric structure, with support reported for a nine-factor model with an additional general factor (i.e., bifactor; <ref type="bibr">Frazier et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These analyses were conducted with both autistic and non-autistic child participants.
Additional reported analyses indicated strict measurement invariance across age groups, sex, race, and ethnicity, providing psychometric support for the nine subscale scores and total score.
In a follow-up study, Frazier and colleagues (2025) used a series of CFAs and ESEMs to replicate their previous psychometric findings.
Support was found for the nine-factor model with an additional general factor.
Additionally, further evidence of scalar invariance was reported across sex, age groups, race, ethnicity, and diagnosis.
No scale structure analytic work could be located for the English version of the CAST.
Gilliam (2014b) used EFA on an autistic sample in the development of the GARS-3 scale.
The results of their factor analysis, which supported a six-factor model, formed the six GARS-3 subscales.

It should be noted that the sample used for the factor analysis included multiple types of informants (e.g. caregivers, teachers, allied health professionals, other family members, advocates and others) and was not limited to primary caregivers of autistic children.
Additionally, the factor analysis is only published in the GARS-3 Examiner's
Manual (Gilliam, 2014b), which is not a peer reviewed source.

text.text: We were not able to locate any peer reviewed studies on the scale structure of the English version of the GARS-3.
No scale structure analytic work could be located for the SCDC.

While Skuse and colleagues (2005) refer to their earlier work (Skuse et al., 1997) as the development of the SCDC and state that this study reports on a PCA, we could not find any indication or mention of a PCA in Skuse and colleagues (1997).

text.text: There was, generally, little description of the development of the SCDC.
Factor analytic work on the SCQ has produced mixed results.
Testing the Lifetime form with participants with a Pervasive Developmental Disorder diagnosis, the original development of the SCQ favoured an EFA-derived four-factor model (Berument et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Testing the Lifetime form with participants with a Pervasive Developmental Disorder diagnosis, the original development of the SCQ favoured an EFA-derived four-factor model <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Berument et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This four-factor model was supported by Wei and colleagues (2015) in their CFA on the Lifetime form (with an autistic sample).
text.formatted: This four-factor model was supported by <ref type="bibr">Wei and colleagues (2015)</ref> in their CFA on the Lifetime form (with an autistic sample).

text.text: However, Wei and colleagues' CFA on the Current form found particularly poor fit for one of the four factors (Social Interaction).

Additional studies have supported a two-factor model (Magyar et al., 2012), using EFA and CFA on the Lifetime form for participants with Down syndrome, with and without autism, and a threefactor model (Grove et al., 2019), using CFA on the Current form with an autistic sample.

text.text: More recently, Ozcan and colleagues (2025) were unable to identify a stable factor structure for the Current form using either EFA or CFA.
Taken together, these findings indicate substantial inconsistency in the latent structure of the SCQ, particularly for the Current form.
While some EFAs and CFAs have supported two-, three-, or four-factor solutions, other studies have been unable to identify a stable factor structure.
To date, research has not examined higher-order or bifactor models to evaluate whether a single total scale score is psychometrically justified.

PCAs on the SRS-2 have yielded results consistent with a single component solution in general population samples (Constantino, Hudziak, et al., 2003 and Wigham et al., 2012) and in a mixed sample of autistic children and children with other psychiatric diagnoses (Constantino et al., 2004).

Constantino and Gruber (2012a) note that while the SRS subscales may be useful for measuring response to interventions, the subscales should not be interpreted individually.

text.text: The development of the SSDS used exploratory ESEM (in autistic participants) and confirmatory ESEM (in non-autistic and other neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric diagnoses groups), with results favouring a five-factor model using 40 of the 58 items (Phillips et al., 2019).

text.text: The five subscales for the SSDS correspond to the five factors identified.
Therefore, while there is psychometric support for using the five subscales, use of a total scale score with all 58 items (or 71 items from the extended version) currently lacks psychometric support.
It is also worth noting the small sample size used for the exploratory ESEM (N = 175).

text.text: Aside from the SCQ and SRS-2, there were limited (or in some instances no) peer reviewed studies on the sensitivity and specificity of included questionnaires.
We summarise key findings below.
An overview of all located studies reporting on the sensitivity and specificity of included questionnaires is presented in Supplementary Table 2.

text.text: For a cut-off score of 5, the ABII-PQ has shown sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 95% (Ward et al., 2017) in differentiating autistic and non-autistic children.

text.text: While the sensitivity of the CAST varied greatly between the Allison and colleagues (2021) and the Williams and colleagues (2005) studies (56% and 100%, respectively), the reported specificity was consistently high (100% and 97%, respectively) in differentiating between autistic and non-autistic samples.

text.text: However, the small autistic sample (n = 9) in Williams and colleagues' study raises questions about the interpretability of their reported sensitivity.
We were not able to locate any peer reviewed studies reporting on the sensitivity and specificity of the GARS-3.

However, the approach taken in the GARS-3 Examiner's Manual (Gilliam, 2014b) to systematically differentiate autism groups (autism only or with cooccurring conditions) from various other groups (non-autistic, ADHD, speech-language impairments, emotional or behavioural difficulties) is commendable. Gilliam (2014b) reported sensitivity and specificity as 96% and 95%, respectively, when differentiating autistic children (without co-occurring diagnoses) from neurotypical peers. Skuse and colleagues (2005) reported that at a cut-off score of 9, the SCDC had sensitivity and specificity of 90% and 69%, respectively, to differentiate between autistic and non-autistic (combination of clinical and non-clinical) samples.

text.text: However, the specificity drops to 35% when differentiating between autistic and non-autistic clinical samples.

Twenty-seven studies reported on the sensitivity and specificity of the SCQ across various cut-off scores (see Supplementary Table 2), with large variations in results and methodology across the 27 studies making it difficult to discern an overall pattern.

The lower overall specificity for the SCQ may be attributable to the complex comparison groups used in most studies (e.g., non-autistic children with other neurodevelopmental conditions).

Eight studies reported on the sensitivity and specificity of the SRS-2 across the multiple specified cut-offs used to indicate different levels of likelihood/severity (60-65 = Mild; 66-75 = Moderate; 76+ = Severe).

Inspection of the ten questionnaires in Table 3 highlights a general tendency for questionnaires to focus on assessing social communication and interaction traits (Criterion A), with some sub-criteria for the restricted and repetitive behaviours (Criterion B) having few, or a complete lack of, items within some questionnaires.

text.text: In the cases of the SCDC and SSDS, the absence of any items relating to Criterion B reflects an intentional focus on Criterion A, as per questionnaire design.
This does not pose an issue if Criterion A is all clinicians or researchers wish to assess.
For clinicians and researchers wanting to assess all DSM-5-TR sub-criteria, the choice would appear to be between the ASDQ and GARS-3.
Six questionnaires included items classified as relating to "more than one" subcriterion.

This either indicates the presence of a double-barrelled item (e.g., "Experienced problems with repetitive behaviours or restricted interests") or an item which relies on the assumption that another sub-criterion is already being met (e.g.
"Engages socially with others but only as part of his/her own routine or preoccupations").
Clearly, items relating to more than one sub-criterion confound one's ability to ascertain which specific trait is being measured.

Similarly, the incidence of "Unclear/None" items may pose a cause for concern given that endorsement of these items could lead to an inflated score for reasons other than having pronounced autistic traits.

text.text: The ABII-PQ had the highest FRE rating (83), with 91% of items deemed to have "Acceptable Clarity".
This reflects the simple language used in the questionnaire.
However, simple language use does not constitute relevance.
For example, while it is easy to understand the item "Do/did you find your child difficult to soothe?", this content is not related to a specific autistic diagnostic sub-criterion.
It is therefore important to keep in mind that while readability and clarity were high, 27% of the ABII-PQ's items could not be sorted into one of the DSM-5-TR autism sub-criteria (see Table 3).

The AIM and GARS-3 did not score well on item clarity.
FRE indicated complex language across these questionnaires (FREs of 53.7 and 50.2, respectively).
Also, some GARS-3 items included technical terms (e.g., "stereotyped" or "affect"), limiting their clarity.
Notably, while the ASDQ has a low FRE, indicating greater reading difficulty, we considered this measure to have high clarity in item wording.
This apparent discrepancy is understandable when one notes the items of the ASDQ often include examples to provide clarity.
This results in longer sentences and subsequently, a lower FRE.
The SSDS 58-item and 71-item versions had FRE scores of 62.7 and 64, and clarity ratings of 93% and 92%, respectively, based on our evaluation.
In addition to our evaluation, Phillips and colleagues (2019) provide further valuable insight into the clarity of the original 58 SSDS items.

Phillips and colleagues reported that 88% of the 175 parent respondents indicated no clarity issues, with 12% suggesting some items were unclear.
Inter-rater reliability between the two non-autistic authors was 82%.
Inter-rater reliability between the non-autistic authors consensus decision and the autistic author was 88%.

text.text: Ninety per cent or more of ABII-PQ, AQ-Child, SCQ, and SSDS items were rated as "Appropriate".
It is noteworthy that the AQ-Child and SCQ received these high ratings for respectful language despite their earlier development dates.

The ABII-PQ and SSDS are among the most recently developed questionnaires, whereas the questionnaires rated lowest for respectful language, the SCDC and the SRS-2 (identical to the original SRS released in 2005), are two of the oldest questionnaires.
Thus, there appears to be a positive trend towards increased use of neutral, respectful and neurodiversity-affirming language over time.
Irrespective of respectfulness rating, questionnaire items generally portrayed autistic traits negatively.

For example, although respectfully worded, the item "Has more difficulty than other children with changes in his or her routine" is portraying a negative side of preference for routines (whereas one could instead ask if a child strongly prefers following routines).
In another instance, playing with toys in ways for which they were not intended (e.g., spinning toy cars) was described by a questionnaire item as "inappropriate".
Similarly, descriptions of differences in speech ranged from "unusual" to "odd" to "abnormal".
Items relating to sensory processing differences often asked if a child was being "overly sensitive" to sensory stimuli.
The use of the term "overly" was considered an unnecessary qualifier which could invalidate a child's distress.

The same issue was raised in recent revisions of the Comprehensive Autistic Trait Inventory, an adult autistic trait questionnaire (English et al., 2021), where community reference groups indicated a preference for alternative phrasing (English et al., 2025; Hechler et al., 2025).

text.text: We suggest these items could be improved by simply removing the term "overly".
Alternatively, another appropriate example is one item in the ASDQ which respectfully assesses sensory processing differences by asking whether the child "dislikes" certain sensory stimuli.
Relatedly, though not directly to do with item wording, is the use of the medicalised word 'symptom' in the title of the ASDQ.
While it is important to acknowledge difficulties and differences, it is still possible to capture these without resorting to ableist or pathologizing language.

Although not captured in our review of item wording, the items of several questionnaires (AQ-Child, CAST, GARS-3, SCDC, SCQ, SRS-2, SSDS) unnecessarily contained gendered pronouns (e.g., "S/he", "him or her").
In addition to complicating the readability, it excludes non-binary people.

Using gender-neutral pronouns may be especially relevant for autistic trait questionnaires, as research indicates autistic people are more likely to be gender-diverse than non-autistic people (e.g., 5.1% of autistic participants expressed gender variance compared to 0.7% of non-autistic participants in Janssen et al., 2016).

Inclusive research with autistic individuals was not reported in the development of any of the included questionnaires.
In terms of including allies, parents of autistic children were included during the development of four questionnaires with parental feedback collected after the development of another questionnaire.

Overall, there was minimal mention of inclusive research.
Where this was done, it appears limited to members of the wider autism community (i.e., parents) rather than autistic people themselves.

text.text: However, it is important to acknowledge that the absence of explicitly described inclusive research practices does not necessarily mean that such practices were not used.
We also cannot be certain that any of the authors are not themselves autistic, as it would have been unconventional for this to be disclosed within academic literature historically.
That said, given the use of inclusive research practices in autism research has grown considerably only recently, it seems unlikely that earlier work was inclusive at any level.
Fortunately, convention is changing.

Leading autism journals now encourage or require authors to include a community involvement statement in research submissions, and emerging research indicates there has been a noticeable increase in the report of inclusive research (Tan et al., 2024).

text.text: In this review we critically analysed ten caregiver-report questionnaires designed for measuring autistic traits in children aged 4 to 12 years.

Each was examined in relation to psychometric support for scale structure, sensitivity and specificity in differentiating autism and non-autism groups, item coverage of DSM-5-TR autism sub-criteria, clarity of item wording, use of respectful and neurodiversity-affirming language, and use of inclusive research practices in questionnaire development.
Progress in understanding autism is likely to be impeded if research is based on questionnaires with inadequate scale-structure support.
However, with the exception of the ASDQ, GARS-3, and SSDS, factor analytic studies did not support purported scale structure for the included questionnaires.
For the ASDQ, GARS-3 and SSDS, the purported subscales were based on factor analyses conducted during scale development.
As the development of the GARS-3 (Gilliam, 2014b) included exploratory analysis only, subsequent factor analytic studies are necessary to support the findings.
text.formatted: As the development of the GARS-3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Gilliam, 2014b)</ref> included exploratory analysis only, subsequent factor analytic studies are necessary to support the findings.

text.text: In contrast, the development of the ASDQ (Frazier, Dimitropoulos, et al., 2023) and SSDS (Phillips et al., 2019) included confirmatory analyses.
text.formatted: In contrast, the development of the ASDQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Frazier, Dimitropoulos, et al., 2023)</ref> and SSDS <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Phillips et al., 2019)</ref> included confirmatory analyses.

text.text: Regardless, further factor analysis conducted by researchers other than the questionnaire developers would still be desirable.

While sensitivity and specificity in differentiating autistic from non-autistic groups are always important considerations, the purpose of using a given questionnaire will influence how stringently one decides acceptable values.

Regardless, well-informed questionnaire selection necessitates several studies investigating sensitivity and specificity across groups with different characteristics and for different purposes (as is the case with the SCQ and SRS-2).

Decisions on using questionnaires for classification or screening are challenging when there are only a few published studies (e.g., as for the ABII-PQ, AQ-Child, ASDQ, CAST, GARS-3, and SCDC), and especially problematic when there is a complete absence of published specificity and sensitivity research (e.g., as for the AIM and SSDS).

Based on the available literature, and striking a balance between sensitivity and specificity in differentiating between autistic and non-autistic children, adequate sensitivity and specificity has been reported for the ABII-PQ, AQ-Child, ASDQ, GARS-3, SCQ (Lifetime form), and SRS-2.

However, when aiming to differentiate between autistic children and children with other neurodevelopmental conditions or behavioural concerns there is considerably less choice due to the limited literature currently available.

For the GARS-3, excellent specificity was reported in differentiating between autistic children and children with other neurodevelopmental conditions; however, the reported specificity for differentiating autistic children from children with behavioural concerns was below adequate (Gilliam, 2014b).

text.text: While the reported specificity for SRS-2 was similarly poor in differentiating autistic children from those with other behavioural concerns, specificity improved to acceptable levels when using the higher cut-off of 76 (Moul et al., 2015).

text.text: Following review of DSM-5-TR autism sub-criteria coverage, the ASDQ and GARS-3 were identified as the most comprehensive questionnaires as they included at least three items for all seven diagnostic sub-criteria.
Alternatively, for clinicians and researchers focused on Criterion A (social communication and interaction traits), the SSDS presents a thorough option.
While the ASDQ and SSDS demonstrated adequate wording clarity, the GARS-3 did not.
This may impact the reliability and validity of the GARS-3, which consequently may impact its usefulness.
Similarly, while the SSDS uses respectful language, the ASDQ and GARS-3 had 15-19% of items that could be improved in this regard.

While language issues may appear inconsequential to some, the accumulation of even slightly judgemental and invalidating descriptions of autistic traits promotes the marginalisation and discrimination of autistic people (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021) and may negatively affect the informants' perception of autism and ratings of autistic features.

text.text: Finally, based on published information in the included studies, inclusive research practices were lacking in questionnaire development, and if present, were likely restricted to members of the wider autism community.
Additionally, where wider community members were included, reported involvement was limited.

Input from parents on the ABII-PQ, AIM, ASDQ, and GARS-3 resulted in some changes to item wording, whereas parental feedback on the SSDS was collected only as a part of initial administration, and therefore after item development.

While input from members of the wider autism community is a welcome and valuable resource, their input should be alongside rather than in place of the input of autistic people (Fletcher-Watson, Brook, et al., 2021).

text.text: To guide developers of future questionnaires, we provide a summary of best practice recommendations.
Some of the desirable features were not expanded upon in the review due to gaps and limitations in the existing literature.
Nonetheless, they are essential for ensuring a robust instrument.
These recommendations are therefore intended to complement the findings of this review and offer guidance for more rigorous scale development.
Initial item development should begin with a clearly defined conceptualisation of the latent construct(s) being measured.
In this review, this conceptualisation corresponded to alignment with DSM-5-TR criteria.
It is also critical that items are worded in a manner that is both clear and respectful.
Clarity ensures that respondents interpret the items consistently, while respectful language may reduce social desirability bias and support neuro-affirming practices.
Inclusive research practices are especially valuable in this phase.

Involving members of the target population, such as autistic people and caregivers of autistic children, can improve the content validity of the item pool and provide essential feedback on item clarity and tone.
Once an initial item pool has been developed, the scale's structure should be examined through appropriate psychometric analyses.
In the absence of an a priori model, EFA is typically the first step, followed by CFA in independent samples.

Continuing from this, invariance testing should be routinely incorporated to determine whether the factor structure holds across key subgroups (e.g., by age, gender, or diagnostic status; Boateng et al., 2018).

text.text: Invariance testing was not a feature of the present review because of the limited existing evidence for most of the included questionnaires.

Nevertheless, the four reported instances of invariance testing are documented in Supplementary Table 1 (Frazier, Dimitropoulos, et al., 2023; Frazier et al., 2014 Frazier et al., , 2025;; Zhong et al., 2023).

text.text: In addition to testing for invariance, the validity of identified factors should be evaluated.

In essence, once research has systematically established a stable factor structure, subsequent research should examine whether the resulting factors show meaningful associations with more direct measures of the purported underlying constructs (i.e., convergent validity; Boateng et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In essence, once research has systematically established a stable factor structure, subsequent research should examine whether the resulting factors show meaningful associations with more direct measures of the purported underlying constructs (i.e., convergent validity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Boateng et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a factor labelled "social motivation"
should ideally correlate with an independent, validated measure of social motivation.
Commendably, Frazier and colleagues (2025) recently reported convergent validity for the factors of the ASDQ.

For questionnaires intended for use in screening or diagnostic contexts, it is essential to systematically evaluate their sensitivity and specificity to differentiate the target population from other relevant groups.

The approach taken in the GARS-3 Examiner's Manual provides an example of good practice in this area, having established its capacity to distinguish autistic children (with and without co-occurring conditions) from those with other developmental or behavioural presentations (Gilliam, 2014b).

text.text: Given diagnostic assessments often integrate information from multiple informants (e.g., caregivers, teachers), future research should also consider whether incorporating questionnaire data from additional sources enhances screening precision.
For instance, it may be useful to investigate whether combined caregiver-and teacher-report questionnaire scores improve the ability to distinguish autism from other neurodevelopmental conditions.

Based on the findings from our review and considering all reviewed characteristics together, it appears that the SSDS may be a good option for clinicians and researchers focusing on Criterion A traits, or the ASDQ for coverage of both Criteria A and B. Both of these measures are freely available, making these questionnaires particularly accessible and therefore appealing.
However, there are also important limitations to consider.
The current psychometric support for the SSDS raises questions about using more than the 40 items from the five factor-derived subscales.
Whereas the ASDQ development bodes strong psychometric support, the low number of items within all but one subscale may be a drawback.
Additionally, it appears that autistic people were not explicitly included in the development of either questionnaire.
To summarise, there is a need for further development of caregiver-report autistic trait questionnaires for use with school-aged children.

As well as ensuring strong psychometric support for scale structure, appropriate sensitivity and specificity, coverage of the diverse range of autistic traits, and clear and respectful use of language throughout (including in the name of the measure, its instructions and items), it is crucial that future questionnaires are developed with autistic people.
